notFound.question: Terminal says a command isn't found. What can I do?
notFound.answer: Some tools put their commands in a folder Terminal doesn't search, so typing one may find nothing, or run another program with the same name. Open a new Terminal window and try again; if it still isn't found, follow the tool's installation instructions. A command's name isn't always the tool's name, and you can search Installed by command. This is judged from the Terminal settings read when this app opened.

missingTools.question: Why are some uv tools missing?
missingTools.answer: uv leaves out tools it can't read, for example when the Python they use is gone. When that happens, a notice says so and the other tools are still listed. To see which tools uv left out and why, run the command in that notice in Terminal. Once the problem is fixed, choose Check Again.

cantUpdate.question: Why can't some tools be updated here?
cantUpdate.answer: On Updates, under the tools that can be updated, a line says how many more can't be updated here; click it to see them, and if a source's list or check is incomplete, Check Tool Setup names that source and can open it while it's still listed. Each of their rows says why, for example “View only”, “Pinned” or “Updates when run”; if a pip package's index rejects the check and no version is confirmed, it says “Can't check”, and you can copy the error details, as you can under Show Error Details when a notice that a check didn't finish offers it, to send to someone who can help. Tools installed with pip, npm packages or Homebrew tools in folders this account can't change, and Ollama models at an address with a login can only be viewed; if OLLAMA_HOST is set to an address that can't be used, no Ollama models are listed, and no other Ollama is contacted instead; dependencies installed inside an npm package aren't offered as separate updates. A pinned tool, a pipx one included, has to be unpinned in Terminal first, and rustup set to get its updates from another address isn't checked or updated here; one marked “Updates when run” updates itself, and opening it can check for a new version if its automatic updates are on, though not always right away.

twins.question: What does “Installed twice” mean, and what should I do?
twins.answer: More than one copy of the same AI coding tool is installed, say once with npm and once by its own installer; only the tools shown under “AI Tools” are checked for this. Typing its command in Terminal runs one of them at most; select the tool, and “In Terminal” can show which one. Updating the copy Terminal doesn't use doesn't change the one it runs, unless the confirmation says the update points the command back to the copy being updated. Uninstalling one copy leaves the other as it is.

password.question: Why is my Mac password needed? Can it be typed for me here?
password.answer: Some apps installed with Homebrew ask for your Mac's login password when they're updated or uninstalled, and the confirmation says so beforehand; the password can't be typed here, and it isn't saved. If that stops one, its View Steps gives a command to copy into Terminal, where you type the password when asked; nothing appears on screen as you type, and that's normal. When it's done, come back here and press ⌘R to check again. After Banager is quit and reopened, an update's View Steps stays on its row for up to 30 days, while the tool still has an update and no later update or successful uninstall of it has taken its place, and in Update History unless you click Clear History; the history keeps only its last 1,000 records, so it can go sooner, and all of this needs the history to be saved, which a warning over Updates says when it couldn't be.

leftBehind.question: What stays behind after uninstalling, and where?
leftBehind.answer: Before uninstalling, the confirmation says what goes and what stays; where that can't be known beforehand, it says so. A tool's settings and data elsewhere are usually kept; where their place is known, it's listed under “Stays after uninstalling” with Copy Path. For the copies Claude Code, Antigravity CLI, Grok Build and Codex installed themselves, the files are moved to the Trash, and you can drag them back; uninstalling rustup deletes its folders for good, without the Trash. Uninstalling with Homebrew leaves the other software installed along with it, unless the confirmation says otherwise.

cantUninstall.question: Why does other software keep a tool from being uninstalled?
cantUninstall.answer: The confirmation lists, under “Software that uses it”, the other software Banager found that still needs the tool, and Uninstall stays off. Tools installed with uv still need it for updates and uninstalling, including when uv itself was installed with pipx. Uninstall Selected keeps one copy of Ollama when the copies selected count on each other for the models listed on this Mac, even when the models are kept outside ~/.ollama/models. Uninstall the tools or models that need it first, then the tool they needed.

changesMac.question: Does this app change my Mac?
changesMac.answer: For an update or uninstall you choose here, the confirmation lets you see the command it will run or the files it will move, and nothing starts until you confirm. The app itself writes three files, all in ~/Library/Application Support/com.brulek.banager: its settings, its record of updates and uninstalls, and the window's size and position; WebKit, the part of macOS that draws the window, can also keep data and a cache for it in folders named com.brulek.banager in ~/Library/WebKit and ~/Library/Caches; the app doesn't edit Terminal's settings files, and it doesn't start version managers' shims, such as mise's or pyenv's, because some install a missing version first, so a tool it finds only through one shows that its program couldn't start. Looking for commands, measuring disk use and scanning for other programs, it doesn't read protected places such as Documents, Desktop, Downloads, iCloud Drive, other disks and network volumes, except two kinds that appear as a folder outside /Volumes: a disk set up that way, and a network volume your home folder is on. The tools it runs change their own files, and sometimes more: checking for updates, Homebrew may first update itself and check online for new versions, and when Homebrew renames something you installed with it, or moves it to another kind of package, it can install, move or uninstall software by itself, without a preview or confirmation; uninstalling rustup removes the line it added to Terminal's settings files, which the confirmation says beforehand.

otherPrograms.question: What's in Other Programs?
otherPrograms.answer: Programs found in folders where commands are usually kept, such as ~/.local/bin and /usr/local/bin, that couldn't be traced to any source here. They're only listed, never changed; to find out what one is, show it in Finder or copy its path. Under the list it says which folders were looked in; protected places aren't read.

sizes.question: How accurate are the sizes?
sizes.answer: They're worked out from the files on disk and rounded, hence “About”. Where some files couldn't be read it says so, and where measuring stopped part-way it says “or more”; either way the real total is larger, and protected places aren't measured. In a total, a file that appears in several tools counts once, and caches aren't included. Some of a uv tool's files take the same disk space as its cache but are still counted, so the tool alone may take less.

majorUpdate.question: Why are some updates marked “Major update”?
majorUpdate.answer: It means the first number of the version goes up, say from 3.x to 4.0, and how the tool is used or set up may change. Tools whose version starts with 0, Ollama models and tools versioned by date aren't marked; for an app that updates itself, the version read from the app is used when available, otherwise Homebrew's recorded version. If you're not sure, choose “Skip This Version”; you'll be reminded when the next version comes out.

updatedWithWarning.question: Why does an update say it has a warning?
updatedWithWarning.answer: The update succeeded, but a step after it needs attention. Choose “View Log” to see what happened and what to do next. If “Notify me when operations finish” is on, the notification counts it as needing attention too.

serviceAfterUpdate.question: Does updating a background service restart it?
serviceAfterUpdate.answer: Updating its files doesn't restart a running service. For a tool set to run with brew services, the update's confirmation and its saved result remind you to restart it if it is still running the old version. This app doesn't check which version the running service is using.

autoCheck.question: When does the automatic check stop?
autoCheck.answer: It's off unless you choose Daily or Weekly for “Check for updates” in Settings; choosing Manually stops it. Checks stop when you quit the app or restart your Mac, until you open it again; closing the window doesn't stop them. While an update or uninstall is under way, no check starts and it looks again 15 minutes later; when every source fails, it waits longer before each try, up to six hours. If your saved settings can't be read, it stays off until you repair or remove the settings file and reopen the app, as Settings explains.

canagerData.question: Where are my settings from Canager?
canagerData.answer: Canager is this app's old name, and its settings from then are kept in another folder, which this app doesn't read, so versions you skipped and tools you chose not to be reminded about may show updates again. To bring those settings over, quit this app and Canager, choose Go > Go to Folder in Finder, open ~/Library/Application Support/com.brulek.canager and copy settings.json, leaving the original there. Then open ~/Library/Application Support/com.brulek.banager the same way, creating that folder if it isn't there, and paste the file only if that folder has no settings.json yet. If it already has one, that file holds this app's own settings, so don't replace it; to use the old settings instead, first move that file into a new, empty folder, then paste.

homebrew.title: Install Homebrew
homebrew.text: Homebrew is installed in Terminal, where you run its installer and type your password. Nothing here runs it or sees the password.
homebrew.olderMacOS: Homebrew supports macOS 15 and later. It can install on macOS {{version}}, but some things may not work.

steps.open: Click Open Terminal. The install command is copied first.
steps.paste: In Terminal, press Command-V, then press Return.
steps.password: When it asks for your “Password”, type this Mac's login password and press Return. Nothing appears as you type.
steps.return: When it says “Press RETURN”, press Return again, then wait. If it installs the Command Line Tools first, that can take several minutes.
steps.done: “Installation successful!” means it's done, and this window notices by itself.

what.script: Downloads Homebrew's official install script from GitHub and runs it. There's no checksum to compare the script with.
what.admin: Makes sure you're an administrator, lists what it will install, and waits for you to press Return.
what.tools: Installs Apple's Command Line Tools first, if this Mac doesn't have them.
what.place: Puts Homebrew in /opt/homebrew, and lets new Terminal windows find it.
what.update: Finally, has Homebrew check online for new versions once. Homebrew's anonymous analytics are on by default; you can turn them off later.

homebrew.waiting: Waiting for Homebrew to be installed…
homebrew.updating: Homebrew is installed and finishing its first update…
homebrew.copyFailed: Couldn't copy the command. Copy it from Show Command instead.

homebrew.name: Homebrew
homebrew.what: The most widely used way to install command-line tools on a Mac
homebrew.more: Every other tool on this page is installed and updated with it. It's installed in Terminal and needs this Mac's login password.

claude-code.name: Claude Code
claude-code.what: Anthropic's AI coding assistant for Terminal
claude-code.more: Writes and changes code when you say in plain words what you want. Once installed, type claude in a new Terminal window.
claude-code.use: Type claude in a new Terminal window.

codex.name: Codex
codex.what: OpenAI's AI coding assistant for Terminal
codex.more: Reads your project and writes or changes code as you ask. Once installed, type codex in a new Terminal window.
codex.use: Type codex in a new Terminal window.

gemini-cli.name: Gemini CLI
gemini-cli.more: Answers questions and works on code in Terminal; installing it also installs Node.js. Once installed, type gemini in a new Terminal window.
gemini-cli.use: Type gemini in a new Terminal window.

ollama.name: Ollama
ollama.what: Runs AI models on this Mac
ollama.more: The models you download run without an internet connection, and they're listed and updated here. Once installed, open Ollama from Applications.

model.name: Gemma 3
model.what: An openly released AI model from Google, chosen for this Mac's memory: {{model}}, about {{size}}
model.more: Once downloaded it runs on this Mac without an internet connection, and answers questions and writes in many languages, Chinese included. Type ollama run {{model}} in a new Terminal window, or use it in the Ollama app.
model.use: Type ollama run {{model}} in a new Terminal window.

node.name: Node.js
node.what: Runs programs written in JavaScript, as many AI tools are
node.more: Tools installed with npm need it, and npm comes with it. Once installed, type node or npm in a new Terminal window.
node.use: Type node or npm in a new Terminal window.

uv.name: uv
uv.what: Installs and runs tools written in Python
uv.more: It keeps each Python tool in a place of its own so they don't clash, and they're listed and updated here. Once installed, type uv in a new Terminal window.
uv.use: Type uv in a new Terminal window.

ffmpeg.name: ffmpeg
ffmpeg.what: Converts and cuts audio and video
ffmpeg.more: Changes a video's format, takes its sound out or cuts a clip with one command. Once installed, type ffmpeg in a new Terminal window.
ffmpeg.use: Type ffmpeg in a new Terminal window.
